edits.title: Let the hand make the connection
edits.incitement: Release-to-connect is an actual action in the artifact. Describe that action plainly before the surprise of the barrier.
edits.old: Two black points wait beside a barrier: **DO NOT CROSS.** Bring them near one another and release to request a connection. Watch for the segment between them. What else moved?
edits.new: Two black points wait beside a barrier: **DO NOT CROSS.** Bring one close to the other, then let go. Watch for the segment that joins them. What else moved?
edits.purpose: Invite the implemented proximity-and-release gesture without introducing request terminology before the consequence.
edits.reader_move: Bring an endpoint close to the other and release it.
edits.why_here: The new relation begins as a small action whose larger consequence can surprise the visitor.
edits.without: The invitation reads like an interaction specification before the reader has an encounter to understand.

edits.title: Explain the invisible part of the barrier
edits.incitement: The visually empty space under the plank was also blocked. The prose needs to distinguish the visible prop from the shape that enforced it.
edits.old: Try crossing where the barrier stood. While intact, its collider reached from the floor to the bar; the visible gap beneath the plank did not let you through. Disconnecting the points does not rebuild it.
edits.new: Try crossing where the barrier stood. Before it broke, an invisible collision shape filled the space from the floor to the bar. The space looked open beneath the plank, but the player could not pass through it. The explosion removes that shape too. Disconnecting the points does not put it back.
edits.purpose: Connect the newly available passage to the removal of a collision shape that occupied more space than the visible plank.
edits.reader_move: Cross the former barrier position and reconsider what had been blocking the simulated body.
edits.why_here: The explosion has just supplied a consequence; its difference from a visual effect can now be explained.
edits.without: A reader can mistake the disappearance of a visible plank for a sufficient explanation of changed movement.

edits.title: Let the earlier room return differently
edits.incitement: A generic invitation to keep a question can become a specific comparison: repeated arrival in Point One and the lasting consequence of a first connection here.
edits.old: There is a whole inquiry waiting there. Keep the question with you as you move to the next pair of endpoints.
edits.new: In the first room, leaving the target made another arrival possible. Here, the first connection leaves a passage open even after the points separate. The rooms keep different things from the gestures we make in them.
edits.purpose: Carry forward the entry-state lesson from Point One while noticing that this room preserves a different consequence.
edits.reader_move: Compare a repeatable arrival with a first connection whose passage remains open.
edits.why_here: The reader has experienced both rules and can compare what persists before proceeding to a continuously measured line.
edits.without: The transition gestures at an inquiry without specifying what the encounters make available to compare.

edits.title: Read the subtraction component by component
edits.incitement: The first displacement calculation benefits from translating its result into the three directions already introduced in Point One.
edits.old: `b - a` gives the displacement from the first position to the second: here, one unit along X. In this room we use that unit as a metre. `length()` gives the magnitude of that displacement, the straight distance between the endpoints.
edits.new: `b - a` subtracts the starting coordinates from the ending coordinates. Here the result is `(1, 0, 0)`: one unit along X, none along Y or Z. In this room we use that unit as a metre. `length()` returns one number for the size of that displacement: `1.0`.
edits.purpose: Explain the vector subtraction and its scalar length through the values in the existing code example.
edits.reader_move: Read each component of the difference and then the one-number length.
edits.why_here: The reader has seen the short code and now needs its operations to be legible.
edits.without: Magnitude and displacement can become vocabulary to accept rather than operations to follow.

edits.title: Read between the same points the other way
edits.incitement: Reversing the subtraction isolates direction from distance without requiring a new artifact or an invented control.
edits.old: Change either position and calculate again. The coordinates can change; we still have two endpoints and the segment between them. We have a small way to describe something that our hands can alter.
edits.new: Reverse the subtraction: `a - b` gives `(-1, 0, 0)`. Its length is still one metre. The points have stayed where they are; the direction between them has changed because we chose the other point as the start.
edits.purpose: Show that the ordered displacement changes when its starting point changes, while the same segment retains its length.
edits.reader_move: Reverse the calculation for the written example, keeping its positions fixed.
edits.why_here: The preceding calculation has established length; reversing it makes direction separately understandable.
edits.without: The instruction to choose A to B remains less consequential than the visible length.
